§2.3 Classical Symmetries

2.3 Classical Symmetries

2.3.1 Classical Symmetries

2.3.1.1 Noether’s Theorem
  • This theorem is the core in the utilizing symmetries in classical and non-classical field theory.

Theorem 2.3.1.1.1 (Noether's Theorem).

If a Lagrangian has a continuous symmetry (i.e. it is parameterizable by some continuous 𝛼), there exists a conserved current 𝐽𝜇 associated with said symmetry when the equations of motion of the Lagrangian are satisfied, i.e. the Euler-Lagrange equations. In other words, symmetries imply conservation laws.

Proof.

The Proof for Noether’s Theorem is fairly short and clever.

We define ℒ︀ as the Lagrangian of the system, 𝜙𝑛 as the field(s) involved in the system, and 𝛼 as the parameter of the continuous symmetry.

Similar to the derivation of the Euler-Lagrange equations,

0=𝛿ℒ︀𝛿𝛼=∑𝑛((𝜕ℒ︀𝜕𝜙𝑛−𝜕𝜇𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙𝑛))𝛿𝜙𝑛𝛿𝛼+𝜕𝜇(𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙))𝛿𝜙𝑛𝛿𝛼)

This expression must be equivalent to zero due to 𝛼 parametrizing a symmetry (i.e. the Lagrangian is invariant wrt some variation in the parameter). It is necessary to define a

𝐽𝜇≡∑𝑛(𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙))𝛿𝜙𝑛𝛿𝛼

Since we are only considering the case in which the equations of motion hold true, (i.e. the Euler-Lagrange equations are true), we have that

𝜕𝜇𝐽𝜇=𝜕𝜇∑𝑛(𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙))𝛿𝜙𝑛𝛿𝛼=∑𝑛𝜕𝜇(𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙))𝛿𝜙𝑛𝛿𝛼=0

Therefore due to some continuous symmetry parametrized by some 𝛼, there exists a conserved current 𝐽𝜇. ⁠□

  • The Energy-Momentum Tensor 𝒯︀𝜇𝜈 is the conserved current for spacetime translation.

Definition 2.3.1.1.2 (Energy Momentum Tensor).

The Energy-Momentum Tensor 𝒯︀𝜇𝜈 for some Lagrangian ℒ︀[𝜙1,𝜕𝜇𝜙1,…𝜙𝑛,𝜕𝜇𝜙𝑛] and some spacetime translation 𝑥𝜈→𝑥𝜈+𝜉𝜈 is defined as

𝒯︀𝜇𝜈≡∑𝑛𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙𝑛)𝜕𝜈𝜙𝑛−𝑔𝜇𝜈ℒ︀
Derivation below.

Starting with the translation

𝜙(𝑥)→𝜙(𝑥+𝜉)=𝜙(𝑥)+𝜕𝜈𝜉𝜈𝜙(𝑥)+…

This provides 𝛿𝜙𝛿𝜉𝜈=𝜕𝜈𝜙 which applies universally regardless of the field 𝜙 (and in fact regardless of the physical object, as it applies to the Lagrangian ℒ︀, a consequence of the fact that 𝛿𝑆=0).

We then have that

𝛿ℒ︀𝛿𝜉𝜈=𝜕𝜇(∑𝑛𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙𝑛)𝛿𝜙𝑛𝛿𝜉𝜈)=𝜕𝜇(∑𝑛𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙𝑛)𝜕𝜈𝜙𝑛)𝜕𝜈ℒ︀=𝜕𝜇(∑𝑛𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙𝑛)𝜕𝜈𝜙𝑛)

We then have that

𝜕𝜇(∑𝑛𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙𝑛)𝜕𝜈𝜙𝑛−𝑔𝜇𝜈ℒ︀)=0

Where we then obtain

𝒯︀𝜇𝜈≡(∑𝑛𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜕𝜇𝜙𝑛)𝜕𝜈𝜙𝑛−𝑔𝜇𝜈ℒ︀)

and 𝜕𝜇𝒯︀𝜇𝜈=0.

  • Energy density:

    ℰ︀=𝒯︀00=∑𝑛𝜕ℒ︀𝜕(𝜙̇𝑛)𝜙̇−ℒ︀
    • 𝜙̇𝑛=𝜕𝑡𝜙𝑛
    • In the case of Lagrangians with 𝜙̇=𝜋=𝜕ℒ︀𝜕𝜙, ℰ︀=ℋ︀ due to the Legendre Transform

Definition 2.3.1.1.3 (4-Momentum).

In terms of the energy-momentum tensor, 4-momentum 𝑝𝜇 is defined as

𝑝𝜈≡∫d3𝑥𝒯︀0𝜈=(𝐸,𝑝⃗)
2.3.1.2 More information on currents
  • A current can refer to a Noether current (such as the ones previously seen)
  • They can be external, such as a moving electron in a wire

  • They can be sources for fields

    • They are never fields with kinetic terms
  • They can be placeholders in Lagrangians

Example 2.3.1.2.1 (Currents in Lagrangians).

In

ℒ︀=−14𝐹𝜇𝜈𝐹𝜇𝜈−𝜙̃□𝜙−𝑖𝑒𝐴𝜇(𝜙̃𝜕𝜇⃡𝜙),

we can write it as

ℒ︀=−14𝐹𝜇𝜈𝐹𝜇𝜈−𝜙̃□𝜙−𝐴𝜇𝐽𝜇
  • Clearly, you can see how currents are used to represent quantities in lagrangians that we do not care for.
